# Sparse Voxel Storage and Chunking


## Overview
Sparse Voxel Storage and Chunking refers to a family of volume data structures designed to store 3D voxel grids efficiently by discarding empty or uniform space [G]. It solves the memory inefficiency of dense grids, where $N^3$ voxels require proportional storage regardless of content, by leveraging spatial sparsity [G]. Unlike dense grids, these methods store only active (non-zero or non-background) elements, often organizing them into fixed-size chunks or hierarchical tiles to enable $O(1)$ or $O(\log N)$ access [S1, unofficial].

## Shared principles
All methods in this family share the core mechanism of separating topology (which voxels exist) from data (what values they hold) [G].

1. **Sparsity Assumption:** The grid assumes that a significant portion of the volume is empty or uniform [G]. Active voxels are stored explicitly; inactive regions return a default background value or are skipped during rendering [S1, unofficial].
2. **Coordinate Mapping:** Voxels are indexed by integer coordinates $(x, y, z)$ [S1, unofficial]. A transform matrix or scale factor maps these integer indices to object-space positions [S1, unofficial].
3. **Block Organization:** To avoid the overhead of storing individual voxel pointers for every active element, active voxels are grouped into blocks (chunks or tiles) [G]. Common block sizes include $8 \times 8 \times 8$ (512 voxels) [S1, unofficial].
4. **Active Status:** Each block or voxel has an active flag [S1, unofficial]. If a block is inactive, it does not store data values, relying instead on the grid's background value [S1, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Sparse Voxel Grid](8021-sparse-voxel-grid.md)
A sparse voxel grid stores active voxels as a list of coordinates and data, indexed by a hash table or spatial tree (e.g., KD-tree, Octree). It solves memory inefficiency by storing only non-zero elements. Unlike chunk-based methods, it may use larger tree nodes or flat lists, relying on the acceleration structure for lookup rather than fixed-size bitmasks. Choose this when the sparsity pattern is irregular and does not align well with fixed grid chunks.

### [Sparse Voxel Chunk Indexing](8606-sparse-voxel-chunk-indexing.md)
This method organizes active voxels into fixed-size $8 \times 8 \times 8$ chunks, each with a 512-bit bitmask indicating occupancy. It provides $O(1)$ access to chunk topology and linear storage for values, avoiding the pointer-chasing latency of deep trees. It is distinguished by its shallow, fixed-depth structure and bit-level precision. Choose this for high-performance ray marching where predictable memory access and low overhead are critical.

### [OpenVDB Volume Grid Storage](14574-openvdb-volume-grid-storage.md)
OpenVDB uses hierarchical tiling (typically $8 \times 8 \times 8$ small tiles) and explicit separation of topology from data. It supports multi-resolution tiling (e.g., $16 \times 16 \times 16$) for larger uniform regions. It is distinguished by its specific implementation of hierarchical tiling and support for smooth transitions in Signed Distance Fields (SDFs). Choose this for VFX pipelines requiring complex boolean operations, multi-resolution support, and integration with existing OpenVDB tools.

### Voxel Cluster Data Model
**Definition:** A data model for storing voxels in clusters of $8^3$, using two representations: a single-bit occupancy grid for visibility buffer generation and an 8-bit index grid for shading [S1, unofficial]. **Steps:** Store voxels in clusters of size $8^3$ [S1, unofficial]. For visibility buffer generation, use a single-bit representation per voxel (1 for solid, 0 for air) [S1, unofficial]. For shading, maintain a second cluster representation storing an 8-bit index per voxel pointing into a material LUT [S1, unofficial]. Index each voxel in a cluster using 9 bits [S1, unofficial]. Index each cluster using 31 bits [S1, unofficial]. **Parameters:** Material LUT size is up to 256 entries [S1, unofficial]. Material LUT properties may contain albedo and roughness [S1, unofficial]. Object extent is always a multiple of 8 voxels in each of the three dimensions [S1, unofficial]. Cluster indexing uses relative x, y, and z offset indices within an object [S1, unofficial]. Object metadata includes transform, index of first cluster, and number of clusters in each axis-direction [S1, unofficial]. Material LUT reuse is handled by objects containing an index into an array of LUTs to avoid duplication [S1, unofficial]. **Layout:** Visibility cluster data occupies $8^3$ bits (one bit per voxel) [S1, unofficial]. Shading cluster data occupies $8^3 \times 8$ bits (one 8-bit index per voxel) [S1, unofficial].

## Background
The concept of sparse voxel storage originated in the need to render large volumetric datasets (e.g., medical imaging, seismic data) that are mostly empty [G]. Early methods used linked lists or hash maps [G]. The introduction of chunk-based indexing (e.g., in Bonxai and OpenVDB) addressed the memory overhead of hash maps and the traversal cost of deep trees by using fixed-size blocks with bitmasks [S1, unofficial]. OpenVDB, developed by DreamWorks Animation, popularized the hierarchical tiling approach for production VFX [S1, unofficial].
